title: The Flawless Surface of Yves Saint Laurent
author: @NewYorker
content:
Toward the end of “Celebration,” a documentary capturing Yves Saint Laurent’s final years as a working designer, we watch him arrive in New York with his business partner and onetime lover, Pierre Bergé, for the 1999 C.F.D.A. Fashion Awards. Bergé—still blustery and energetic at sixty-eight—flanks Saint Laurent protectively as the two leave their hotel for the ceremony, where the designer is set to receive a lifetime-achievement award. Saint Laurent was only sixty-two at the time, but he looks much older: frail and uncertain in his tuxedo, he totters down a hallway, anxiously licking his lips and smoothing back his too-thick cap of shoe-polish-brown hair. “It’ll be better in three hours,” Bergé tells him, as if reassuring a child.

Onstage, Saint Laurent gives a short thank-you speech in halting English. Designers like himself, he says, must behave like artists, “sacrificing everything, sometimes even our lives, to devote ourselves only to our work.” The audience gives him a standing ovation, and Bergé appears cautiously relieved. But as Saint Laurent begins to make his unsteady way out of the banquet hall, Bergé rushes to his side, to help him. “He’ll fall,” he frets.

“Celebration,” which was directed by the French filmmaker Olivier Meyrou, does a keen, subtle job of exploring the fissures between image and reality—between how things appear and how they, in fact, are. Saint Laurent, who died in 2008, was perhaps one of the twentieth century’s greatest designers. The creator of vivid, indelible fantasies for women to try on and to embody was also a fragile and anguished man, troubled throughout his life by alcohol, drug dependency, and bouts of debilitating depression. The documentary pays tribute to the designer’s genius: the seductive, unfussy flair of his designs is evident, for instance, in footage from the monumental 1998 fashion show that Yves Saint Laurent staged at the Stade de France, in order to commemorate the FIFA World Cup. But the film’s title is ultimately ironic. We watch as Saint Laurent is hustled, with some effort, from one task to the next by members of his team, who attempt, not always successfully, to put a brave face on things. He is still sketching his designs, still offering faint thoughts on the creations that the petites mains—the house’s master seamstresses and artisans—will execute, but he seems almost entirely lost in his own world. Rather than a celebration, the film plays more like a funeral procession, or perhaps a bedside vigil for a man who has, indeed, seemingly sacrificed his life in pursuit of his art. It’s a harrowing portrayal, and it’s not entirely surprising that after a single screening of the film, in 2007, Bergé sued over an unauthorized image, blocking the movie’s release for more than a decade.

title: Her Rape Kit Had a DNA Match. In San Francisco, That’s Not Enough.
author: Seyward Darby
content:
The San Francisco Police Department cleared 14 percent of rape cases last year—half the national rate. An investigation finds that rape kits get tested fast, only for cases to be quietly shelved. Often, the only thing standing “between a report and the shelf” is what’s known as a “pretext call,” a recorded phone conversation in which a survivor tries to extract an admission of guilt from their attacker (aka relives their trauma to do the police’s work for them):

She sat in a room at the SVU headquarters with [Sergeant Johnathan] Ng and a recorder. She dialed the man she alleged raped her. He didn’t pick up. She tried again. No answer.

“If we don’t get an admission, it’s a he-said, she-said thing,” she remembered Ng telling her.

Then, she said, he offered some unsolicited advice.

“He told me that I probably shouldn’t be hanging out with 55-year-old men,” she said.

title: How to Survive an Infestation of Toxic Caterpillars
author: @NewYorker
content:
The oak processionary caterpillar, which is spreading as Europe warms, fills the air with microscopic hairs that inflict excruciating rashes.

July 31, 2026

June 27th, the hottest day ever recorded in Berlin, where I live, began with a whimper. My apartment does not have air-conditioning, and neither does a friend’s garden cottage where I took refuge, so my poor, panting greyhound was audibly distressed. I walked her to a park to cool off. At the entrance, I passed a sign that warned of the presence of Eichenprozessionsspinner, caterpillars with stinging hairs that German news outlets have called a “citywide plague.” The government was hiring workers in protective suits to vacuum them up. I wasn’t too worried, though. Germans often overreact to animal nuisances with complicated schemes. Who else would try to clean nature with a Hoover?

The oak processionary caterpillar, as it is known in English, is a squiggle of dark skin covered in wiry white hairs that look like the whiskers on a witch’s warts. But you never see just one caterpillar. Oak processionary caterpillars live with hundreds or thousands of their siblings, and together they look more like a wizard’s beard. The caterpillars move in a single-file line—a procession—and often defoliate oak trees completely. I saw no bare branches or caterpillars in the wooded area where my dog and I found shelter. We cowered in the shade as the temperature rose to a hundred and four degrees.

As I soon learned, you don’t need to touch these caterpillars to experience their sting. The next morning, a galaxy of itchy red bumps and blotches stretched from my shoulder to my hip. Oak processionary caterpillars have not only tufts of visible hairs but also eight hundred thousand microscopic hairs that, according to one study, can be “projected in the air as a fine powder” when a caterpillar is threatened. These hairs are toxic, and they can travel several hundred metres, survive for years on surfaces, and pass through clothing to impale skin. The entomologist Justin O. Schmidt once developed a scale for the pain inflicted by insects, describing a particularly excruciating wasp sting like so: “Torture. You are chained in the flow of an active volcano.” On a scale for itchiness, my Eichenprozessionsspinner rash would outrank all the mosquitoes, spiders, fleas, and midges that had ever bitten into my flesh. I was reminded of bedbug bites that I once suffered on a forearm, after going to a movie theatre in New York City—but the caterpillar stings covered half my body.

The heat wave broke, but the itching lasted another week. I slathered myself in ointments, even after reading a study that said treatment “shows scarce efficacy” for my condition. The main consolation I took from the scientific literature was that it could have been worse. A caterpillar hair in the eyeball can create a crusty yellow nodule that requires professional removal. In some cases, inhaling the hairs may make it difficult to breathe. Guests at a nineteenth-century dinner party suffered “a disgusting, unbearable itching and scratching in the throat” after they feasted on roasted cuckoos that had preyed on Eichenprozessionsspinner. Worst of all was the plight of a forty-six-year-old Italian farm worker who apparently masturbated after handling processionary-caterpillar nests, as described in an old dermatological case study. The scarring from his injuries was so severe that he needed to be circumcised.

Now that oak processionary caterpillars had my attention, I realized that they were not a parochial German pest. Britain has had them since 2006, when London imported infested oaks from the Continent. Lately, the species has been spilling from Germany into Denmark for the first time. The Netherlands, where they have long been present, recorded a doubling of infested oak trees compared with last year, and Switzerland’s forest-research institute called 2026 “an exceptionally strong Eichenprozessionsspinner infestation year.” France has been beset not only with these caterpillars (processionnaire du chêne) but also with a closely related species that has spread northward from the Mediterranean: the processionnaire du pin, or pine processionary caterpillar. A friend of mine, whose university campus in Nuremberg was infested with Eichenprozessionsspinner, told me, “I think nature is trying to destroy us.”

Toxic caterpillars, like deadly heat waves, are becoming a regular part of European summers. Eichenprozessionsspinner love warm, dry, and sunny springs, and the spring of 2026 was the sunniest in Berlin’s history. Heat and solar radiation not only help oak processionary caterpillars survive after they hatch but also make them trigger-happy with their hairs in summer. “The overall trend will likely lean toward an increasing probability of mass outbreaks,” Thomas Sobczyk, a forest engineer who studies the caterpillars and the moths they turn into, told me in an e-mail. “From my perspective, there’s no alternative to coming to terms with the oak processionary moth’s presence in residential areas.”

After I recovered, I visited Volkspark Jungfernheide, one of Berlin’s largest parks and the site of one of the worst outbreaks in the area. It was nearly empty of people. Workers had been vacuuming up caterpillars for weeks. They wore ventilated face masks and, on each hand, multiple gloves that were duct-taped to their sleeves. I no longer viewed these men and women as caricatures of German overzealousness but as frontline heroes who should be applauded from balconies and open windows. Their vacuum cleaners had originally been designed to suck asbestos out of old buildings; a vacuum bag could hold forty pounds of caterpillars and their nests, and a worker could fill three bags a day.

In June, the city’s twelve districts asked the Berlin Senate, which had been slashing city services for years, to declare the caterpillars a public-health threat, which would have unlocked extra funding and made it easier to use regulated pesticides. The request was denied. The state secretary for the environment said that no one could have predicted the extent of this year’s outbreak, even though the numbers of Eichenprozessionsspinner had climbed every year since 2023. As a result, the districts could do little else but remove caterpillar nests—commonly called “tents”—from trees. The district that encompasses the park, Charlottenburg-Wilmersdorf, had closed playgrounds and sports facilities, including a swimming pool. Caterpillar hairs floated on the water’s surface, leaving swimmers with a necklace of red stings.

At a little biergarten that featured an outdoor theatre, I met an arborist named Gernot von Lyskowski. His firm, GvL, was one of three companies sucking up the caterpillar tents. “We haven’t had it this bad before,” he told me. “We’ve been fighting here in Jungfernheide for four or five years now.” Von Lyskowski originally became an arborist because he loved climbing trees when he was a kid. “We weren’t even aware of what was causing the itching back then,” he said. The caterpillars are not unknown to Germans: in the fifties, for example, hundreds of people attending a festival broke out in rashes after they hid from a downpour under infested trees. Yet the species was uncommon enough that, in 1993, conservationists classified the species as “threatened with extinction” in Berlin. Perhaps today’s Eichenprozessionsspinner outbreak is less like a foreign invasion than like a revolution, in which a lowly element rises up to dominate ecosystems of which it has always been a part.

Between 2003 and 2010, as humans heedlessly dumped unprecedented amounts of carbon dioxide into the atmosphere, the amount of sunshine during the caterpillar’s larval and moth phases was eleven per cent higher in Berlin than it had been two decades prior. During that same time, the caterpillars became commonplace in every district of the city. “It really came on quite suddenly fifteen years ago,” von Lyskowski said. When he started removing Eichenprozessionsspinner, he climbed trees with a twenty-metre-long hose that was connected to a vacuum on the ground. Now he owns three trucks with pneumatic outriggers and aerial lifts which cost two hundred thousand euros each. The caterpillars had been good for business, but he didn’t love the work. “We should be earning much more money from this danger,” he said. A single old oak could contain dozens or hundreds of tents, and each tent could contain hundreds or thousands of caterpillars, which translates into tens of billions of stinging hairs.

Oak processionary caterpillars are nocturnal, and they spin tents out of silk in part so they have a place to digest their food. By early summer, the tents sag like dirty diapers from the undersides of boughs. During my visit to Volkspark Jungfernheide, the caterpillars were already beginning to pupate in the soiled tents. In three to five weeks, they would emerge from their cocoons as brown moths, which could fly several kilometres to lay eggs. When caterpillars first hatch, in the spring, they need a few weeks to develop their stinging hairs. That is the time to hit them with insecticides.

Some parts of Germany are already spraying oak processionary caterpillars with chemicals that are strictly regulated under environmental-protection laws. But there are more than three hundred and sixty species of caterpillar that live on oak trees in Germany, and these insecticides can kill many of them too. Meanwhile, a 2013 study found that the two most common agents “were practically ineffective” against oak processionary caterpillars; the authors speculated that intense solar radiation, the very thing the caterpillars loved, reduced their effectiveness. A more recent British study found that sprayed areas were infested again after one or two years.

Von Lyskowski and his workers sprayed some trees with nematodes, a parasitic worm that kills caterpillars and reproduces inside their carcasses. They cause far less collateral damage to other insects, but they are themselves living, sensitive creatures. They can only be applied on dry, windless nights, and two applications are needed to make a dent in caterpillar populations. “You won’t fully control it with nematodes,” von Lyskowski said. “But at least you get the population down somewhat.” The expert consensus seems to be that we cannot defeat processionary caterpillars. We can only learn to keep our distance from them. “There’s a mistaken belief that we can sustainably influence the population using technical methods—plant protection products or biocides, for instance,” Sobczyk, the forest engineer, said in his e-mail to me. “In the long run, natural factors play a far greater role in population fluctuations.”

If the caterpillars are here to stay, is it possible to learn to love them, at least a little? The nineteenth-century German lepidopterist Jacob Hübner named their genus Thaumetopoea, from the ancient Greek words for “wonder” and “create,” perhaps because he admired their single-file processions and silken nests. I could muster a little wonder, too, when I read that caterpillars evolved stinging hairs more than twenty million years ago and radiated across the Eastern Hemisphere. In the Middle East, processionary caterpillars feed on pistachio trees. In Australia, they specialize in acacias and eucalyptuses; in the Himalayas, Alnus nepalensis and rhododendron leaves. Caterpillars cause health problems there, too. A seasonal blindness in Nepal has been linked to caterpillar hairs.

Sometimes I told myself that caterpillars deserve a chance to defend themselves. Nature targets few other organisms with such cruelty. Charles Darwin said that he could no longer believe in God after he watched a parasitic wasp inject its eggs into a living caterpillar. When they hatched, the wasp larvae slowly ate the caterpillar from the inside, leaving the vital organs for last to keep the caterpillar alive for as long as possible. Maybe caterpillars need to make entire forests uninhabitable just to find a little peace. (Caterpillar-eating predators have evolved defenses of their own—cuckoos and tits, for example, have strategies for neutralizing the stings—but neither bird has checked the caterpillars’ populations.)

In theory, humanity’s carbon emissions could warm the planet too much even for oak processionary caterpillars. Paula Halbig, a scientist affiliated with the Forest Research Institute in Baden-Württemberg, said that if oak processionary caterpillars began hatching too early in the spring, there would be no oak leaves on the trees for them to eat. On the other hand, oak leaves have also started sprouting earlier, because of climate change. And, on the other other hand, warmer winters could accelerate the northward spread of pine processionary caterpillars, which are already invading southern Germany. “It is difficult to find another insect which is so specialized in exploiting climatic conditions,” Andrea Battisti, an Italian entomologist who has been studying pine processionary caterpillars for more than forty years, told me. The ancient Romans apparently ground their hairs into an excruciating poison. Roman soldiers have been said to have tortured prisoners by tossing them into caterpillar pits.

In the nineteenth century, Jean-Henri Fabre, a French entomologist, conducted a famous experiment with pine processionary caterpillars. He coaxed a group of caterpillars into a procession around the rim of a flowerpot, so that each caterpillar both led and followed the others. He expected them to break off at some point in search of food, but, in the end, they mindlessly circled the flowerpot for seven days and then dropped dead from starvation. Fabre took his experiment as proof that scientists would never find “the origin of reason in the dregs of the animal kingdom.” Later, though, his experiment became a metaphor for the dangers of groupthink. As a species that spews toxins into the air by burning fossil fuels, perhaps we humans should feel a certain kinship with these creatures. We might never find the origins of reason in caterpillars, but we may recognize the dregs of the animal kingdom in ourselves. ♦

title: Marvel Tokon: Fighting Souls had a Magik-al open beta weekend, as character popularity data reveals a surprising community favourite
author: Connor Makar
content:
It's a kind of…

The data is in! Following the weekend open beta for Marvel Tokon: Fighting Souls, one player has done the work and discovered which character was the most popular among enthusiastic players.

Fighting game player and webtoon creator AlietteFaye gathered data on character usage from players at Vibranium rank and higher, and found that Magik proved the most popular character. In second place came Blade, then Magneto, followed by Spider-Man.

Magik was also the most popular character in the leader position in teams (meaning the character you start a match using). Black Panther took the third place spot here, with the second and fourth spot filled by Spider-Man and Blade again.

As for the least popular characters, it looks like Danger is down at the bottom. Ms Marvel comes in second-to-last, and then Captain America comes third from the bottom. That itself is surprising, as he is the tutorial character and the closest to a Jack-of-all-trades on the cast.

For clarity, Vibranium rank is the second-highest tier available in the beta, meaning the players whose accounts were analysed would have been especially keen players over the weekend. It's entirely possible these figures will be different if all players were looked at, though that's probably too much work for a single person given how popular it seemed to be.

These dedicated players would have had to tackle some technical problems, sadly. On PC, gameplay and performance problems ran amok for a portion of the playerbase, something Arc System Works has apologised for. Meanwhile, PlayStation players had to take a break from the game during a PSN outage which kept them from jumping online.

Magik coming in at the number one spot is an interesting result, considering the arcane mutant is a relatively unknown character among casual Marvel fans - especially compared to your Iron Mans and Captain Americas. She's proven a fan-favourite among those in the know, however. Still, with a cool new design and a big sword, it looks like there might be… Magik in the air? Sorry, sorry.

title: Payloads used to dictate the terms of launch. That's finally changing.
content:
Chicken or egg?

“The Starship Pez dispenser demonstrates very smart industrial design and scale.”

Artist's illustration of Starship releasing a Starlink V3 satellite from its "Pez dispenser" deployment system. Credit: SpaceX

It wasn’t easy to find anyone outside of SpaceX clamoring for a rocket like Starship just 10 years ago. Today, the space industry can’t wait for Starship to finally deliver.

With a payload capacity of more than 100 metric tons (220,000 pounds) to low-Earth orbit, SpaceX’s new rocket is changing the thinking of just about everyone in the space industry. With the unrealized but potentially game-changing benefits of refueling, Starship could carry the same amount of payload to higher orbits, the Moon, or Mars.

It’s important to note that Starship is still very much in its experimental phase, far from proving Elon Musk’s loftiest claims about what it can do. Still, NASA and the US military are considering novel ways to use Starship to fly to the Moon or transport cargo to far-flung war zones. Scientists are eager to use its enormous volume to launch giant space telescopes. Competitors are taking notice. China, the strongest strategic adversary America has ever faced, is looking for its own Starship. Now, some US satellite manufacturers are adapting for the substantial capacity of the world’s most powerful rocket.

This is a reversal of how things usually go in the balance of supply and demand between launch vehicles and satellite operators. Rocket designs have long engineered their vehicles to match trends in the satellite industry. They designed for their customers’ needs, or at least for what their customers were telling them they needed. But in 2026, a new era of abundant super-heavy-lift launch promises to unlock entirely new applications for satellites.

Historically, engineers relied on a few basic assumptions when it came time to design a new rocket. One was that their launch vehicle would deliver a single payload or a small number of satellites to space. These payloads would be stacked on top of their launch vehicle for release at just the right moment, in just the right orbit. Matching satellites and rockets followed a predictable, orderly pattern. Small satellites needed a small rocket, and larger payloads required a heavier launcher.

Perhaps the most fundamental assumption was that these satellites would ride to orbit inside the uppermost part of the rocket, protected by a clamshell-like aerodynamic shroud that would peel away once the launch vehicle soared above the atmosphere and reached the sterile environment of space.

The only launch vehicle to ever challenge these assumptions was NASA’s Space Shuttle, which deployed numerous satellites of all sizes in the first half of its career before it proved a commercial failure. NASA then turned its focus to constructing the International Space Station, a task the Space Shuttle marvelously completed upon retiring in 2011. Ultimately, the Shuttle was outclassed, at least on a commercial basis, by lower-cost expendable rockets. Its unique attributes never had much influence on how engineers designed their satellites.

Today, SpaceX’s Starship rocket is again promising to upend the launch industry and, by extension, the futures of those who build and own satellites. There are other super-heavy-lift rockets coming onto the market, too. Blue Origin’s New Glenn rocket, particularly a yet-to-fly upgraded variant with more engines, fits in between SpaceX’s workhorse Falcon 9 rocket and Starship.

Taking advantage

Starship’s first real payloads will be SpaceX’s own next-generation Starship V3 broadband satellites. It can carry up to 60 of them on a single launch. Starlink V3s are based on the same stackable, flat-satellite architecture as SpaceX’s existing Starlink satellites.

SpaceX shunned the conventional boxy satellite designs pretty much everyone else has used for more than a half-century. On the Falcon 9, stacks of Starlink satellites still ride to space on top of the rocket, inside a fairing, and then release all at once upon reaching orbit. The company first showed the utility of the flat-packed, stackable satellite architecture with Starlink beginning in 2019.

SpaceX uses a different approach on Starship, with Starlinks riding inside the vehicle’s fuselage, then ejecting through a small door on the side like a Pez dispenser. Pulleys and cables lower each satellite into position for deployment, one at a time, then the door closes to allow the rocket to come back to Earth.

SpaceX settled on this novel architecture for several reasons. The flat design allows each satellite to have a broader surface area facing the Earth. It also eliminates the need, at least initially, for SpaceX to focus on developing a large payload fairing. Rocket Lab’s smaller medium-class Neutron rocket takes a similarly revolutionary approach to payload fairing design, integrating it with the Neutron’s reusable booster stage rather than the expendable upper stage. With Starship, however, SpaceX intends to make the entire vehicle rapidly reusable.

Other satellite manufacturers are starting to take note, but not all of them. Satellites for China’s Qianfan broadband megaconstellation use a flat-panel, stackable design. Amazon’s broadband constellation, Amazon LEO, uses a more conventional-looking satellite.

Muon Space, a satellite manufacturing startup, announced earlier this month that it is developing a new high-power satellite design to take advantage of Starship’s payload accommodation. Muon Space calls the new platform Condor-Ultra. The company says it is “optimized for stackable mass-deployment from SpaceX’s Starship” for potential use on communications, sensing, and orbital data center-type missions.

“It is designed for stackable deployments through the opening without requiring the whole fairing to open,” said Greg Smirin, president of Muon Space. “That’s sort of what we’re designing to, what us and other customers have an understanding of for [what SpaceX will offer in] the near term, in the sort of ’28 timeframe.”

Muon’s new satellite design can also fit on medium-lift rockets, such as the Falcon 9 and Rocket Lab’s Neutron. It will weigh about 1.5 metric tons, or 3,300 pounds, at launch.

Smirin said the diversity of future space missions will require some satellites to take more conventional shapes, some of which will need to launch on a rocket with a more conventional payload fairing. SpaceX is expected to eventually offer a different deployment system to accommodate other kinds of payloads that are not compatible with the Pez dispenser.

“There will likely be some other configurations,” Smirin said in an interview with Ars. “This particular one is absolutely designed to work with the Pez dispenser framework. It sort of maps to the high nadir-facing payload face that you want for Earth interaction, that could also work with a stackable Pez dispenser sort deployment.”

Other satellite manufacturing startups are making inroads in flat-panel designs. Last year, Apex announced a new flat satellite chassis called Comet. On its website, the company teases an even larger version of Comet, named Comet XL, “optimized for Starship and the super-heavy launchers of the future.”

Terran Orbital, a commercial satellite builder owned by Lockheed Martin, also boasts a flat-packed satellite design it calls Enterprise. Vast, best known for its plans to launch a privately funded space station, said last month that it’s branching out into satellite manufacturing. The new initiative, called Vast Satellite, is based on a flat-panel design “for high-density launch and batch deployment.”

John Rood, CEO of the space infrastructure and transportation company Momentus, told Ars he credits SpaceX with the “forethought” of thinking creatively about how to better integrate satellites with their rockets. Momentus specializes in building spacecraft to host small experiments or other customer payloads. For example, the company’s newest mission is now in orbit with NASA- and US military-sponsored experiments to test rendezvous navigation sensors and demonstrate how to robotically assemble modular structures in space.

Momentus’ spacecraft can also serve as space tugs to ferry smaller satellites or experiments from one orbit to another. These kinds of missions aren’t necessarily the best fit for a flat-panel satellite.

“I don’t think it’ll be the new industry norm,” Rood said of the flat-panel architecture. “I think, for obvious reasons, given SpaceX’s heft, it is something that will become a bigger and bigger part of the industry, but I don’t know if everything will transition to that… There are compelling reasons to have other types of satellites.”

Just a tank of gas

A new report from the Aerospace Corporation helps elucidate why satellite companies are optimizing for Starship. It’s big and reusable, and once operational, it could cut the cost of launching a kilogram of payload into orbit by an order of magnitude from the Falcon 9. This means costs could come down from a few thousand dollars per kilogram to a few hundred.

Karen Jones, a space economist and lead author of the paper, said her research supports some of those optimistic cost projections. She outlines three scenarios, two of which assume an initial launch cost of $100 million for each fully reusable Starship and Super Heavy booster, with marginal costs of 20 or 35 percent. This is in line with the marginal costs of the smaller, partially reusable Falcon 9, which SpaceX can launch for as little as $15 million per flight on a dedicated Starlink mission.

This would bring the per-kilogram launch cost for a fully loaded Starship down to $133 to $233 after 10 reuse cycles. A more optimistic scenario with a $50 million initial launch cost and 20 percent marginal cost would reduce payload costs to $67 per kilogram for a Starship/Super Heavy launch at full capacity after nine use cycles. That’s less than it costs to fill the gas tanks of most SUVs. If SpaceX can make these more optimistic ambitions a reality, it would validate a claim made by Elon Musk in 2022 that a Starship flight could eventually cost as little as $10 million.

“I actually thought I would basically disprove that [claim], and on my first try, I got to $67 per kilogram after nine use cycles,” Jones told Ars. “It’s based upon some significant assumptions in the paper, but it’s not something that’s completely crazy. It certainly wouldn’t be something they’d reach on the first few times, on their first model; but over time, and with a learning curve, why not? I think it’s possible.”

In the paper, Jones writes that SpaceX could achieve these numbers “through a combination of manufacturing and operational learning curves, lower marginal costs, a fully laden rocket, and adequate reuse.” SpaceX has shown it can do it with Falcon 9, but it won’t happen overnight with Starship. Earlier this month, SpaceX launched one of its reusable Falcon 9 boosters for a record-setting 35th time. The company reached nine flights of one booster in 2021, nearly 11 years after the very first Falcon 9 launch.

Ordinary to extraordinary

The first obvious market for Starship to serve will be megaconstellations, beginning with SpaceX’s own. These kinds of missions will help SpaceX bend the learning curve to create and enable still-unrealized markets, like routine trips to the Moon and Mars, orbital data centers, or point-to-point transportation on Earth.

“The here-and-now revenue generation opportunities lie with broadband constellations and connectivity plays, basically building out their current constellations,” Jones said. “We focus on megaconstellations. They can kind of grow the business, and then from that platform, and from that success, some of these more speculative ventures might be able to springboard from that.”

In other words, the ordinary will unlock the extraordinary, Jones said.

So it’s no surprise that some satellite manufacturers are thinking seriously about taking advantage of Starship as soon as possible.

“A FlatSat form factor is going to replace these traditional boxy satellites, and a FlatSat type of form factor will help reduce drag and increase maneuverability,” Jones said. “The actual deployment mechanism, which is the Starship Pez dispenser, to me, this demonstrates very smart industrial design and scale. These FlatSats fit into the Pez dispenser, and this could be perhaps the future space de facto standard for rideshare and mass-produced satellites and constellations.

These “FlatSats” are not a panacea. It’s hard to imagine some missions fitting on a flat-panel design. “It’s not to say that there wouldn’t be other types of satellites and ways to launch telescopes and other types of form factors,” Jones said.

But flat-packed, stackable satellites allow operators to deliver more capability to orbit faster. Starship will take this to the next level with its capacity to launch SpaceX’s more powerful Starlink V3s.

“On a Falcon 9, they can only launch 27 of these V2s,” Jones said. “The Starship can launch 60 of these larger V3s. What this means is bandwidth per launch amounts to 61,000 gigabits per second on Starship versus 2,600 gigabits per second for V2s on Falcon 9. In other words, almost 24 times as much bandwidth can be deployed per launch on Starship versus the Falcon 9 and the V2 satellites. That’s huge.”

Of course, costs are not the same as prices. SpaceX charges commercial customers $74 million for a dedicated Falcon 9 launch, about five times the internal launch cost. This still makes Falcon 9 the most affordable and reliable launch option in the Western world. It’s too early to know where or when SpaceX will set Starship launch prices. Part of the calculation will hinge on the progress of SpaceX’s competitors, such as Blue Origin.

“Certainly, that’s what the industry wants to see, is two equal players,” Jones said. “It absolutely contributes to the economics in terms of price per kilogram.”

“We’ve got these two rocket companies vying for positions,” Jones said in an interview. “I think it’s going to be important that we have competition here, and one company seems to be ahead right now, but whether you’re first to market or a fast follower, I think we would all benefit from seeing this competition between these two companies, Blue Origin and SpaceX. I think that’s critical.”

Some economists believe Starship is simply too big to fulfill all of SpaceX’s lofty goals, but Jones doesn’t buy it.

“Sometimes, when you increase the size of any type of transportation system, it creates something called diseconomies of scale, where the marginal costs start to increase,” Jones said. “Now, I think Starship is going to prove a new price point, but some think that when you get too big, kind of like the [Airbus] A380 airplane that tried to compete with the [Boeing] 747, it created all sorts of demands and types of maintenance.

“Could the Starship follow that path and become not relevant? I don’t really believe it,” she said. “I think that they’re going to have to prove it. They’re going to have to prove over time that they can fly the Starship and continue to see marginal costs decrease, and hopefully the space sector will discover a new sweet spot, but right now it’s the Falcon 9.”

Stephen Clark is a space reporter at Ars Technica, covering private space companies and the world’s space agencies. Stephen writes about the nexus of technology, science, policy, and business on and off the planet.

title: Appendix to Barriers and Safeguards: Access to Assisted Dying for the Socioeconomically Vulnerable Harvard Law Review
author: @HarvLRev
content:
A Comprehensive Descriptive Means

  • Volume 139
  • Issue 8
  • June 2026

Where jurisdictions have not yet clarified their stances as to particular safeguards, this Appendix characterizes their approaches as “Unclear.” If a jurisdiction imposes a waiting period but waives it in certain cases, this Appendix categorizes the jurisdiction as imposing the waiting period restriction. This is because exemptions are offered on a case-by-case basis,1 so default waiting periods are barriers to access in themselves because patients are unable to predict, at the time they choose to initiate the assisted dying process rather than to engage in self-help, whether they will be eligible. In the context of assisted dying, advance directives allow competent patients to issue written statements authorizing health care providers to provide or administer fatal medication at a later date, when they may have lost decisionmaking capacity.2

title: UN High Commissioner warns of deepening peril for civil liberties as Uganda tightens restrictions
content:
News

UN High Commissioner warns of deepening peril for civil liberties as Uganda tightens restrictions

UN High Commissioner for Human Rights Volker Türk on Thursday condemned the growing crackdown on fundamental freedoms in Uganda, raising concerns about the erosion of the rule of law in the country and increasing military involvement in civilian institutions, which contribute to a shrinking of civic space.

In commenting on the current state of domestic affairs within the country, Türk stated:

“I am appalled that the authorities are increasingly targeting any form of dissent, and deepening restrictions on the fundamental freedoms of all those living in Uganda…” He added that the authorities’ actions are fostering a climate of fear among citizens, which increases self-censorship and further restricts public debate, thereby deepening polarisation.

The UN reported that repression against opposition figures in Uganda has escalated since the general elections that were held on January 15. Based on information received by the UN Human Rights Office, at least 50 opposition figures, five human rights defenders, and five journalists have experienced various human rights violations, including enforced disappearances, arbitrary arrests, torture, and ill-treatment. The Human Rights Office has also stated that it had information about increased military involvement in the functions of civilian institutions, with some media outlets forced to close temporarily.

Furthermore, Türk criticised the promulgation of special legislation that targets civic space by imposing restrictions on engagement with civil society organizations and international funding, such as the Protection of Sovereignty Act enacted in May 2026. This bill monitors the political activity of foreign actors, regulations foreign funding, and establishes a registration system for any person deemed an “agent of a foreigner.” Rights organizations have previously criticized the Act for its broad provisions and for limiting freedom of speech and peaceful assembly.

Consequently, Volker Türk called on the government to abide by its obligations under the Ugandan constitution as well as international law, including the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights and the African Charter on Human and Peoples’ Rights. He also urged the government to uphold the separation of powers and the rule of law, and to leverage economic opportunities from Uganda’s resources with the support of international funding.

The human rights situation in Uganda has attracted global attention since the January 15, 2026 general elections, which were marked by social and political unrest, including an Internet shutdown, restrictions on freedom of assembly, and clashes between security forces and opposition supporters. The National Unity Platform, a Ugandan political party, rejected the election results, claiming irregularities during the election process. Additionally, in May 2026, Amnesty International reported an increase in restrictions imposed on journalists and media freedom in many countries across East and Southern Africa, including Uganda.

title: Forget Albums—Pop Stars Measure Their Careers in Eras Now
author: @NewYorker
content:
Earlier this year, Charli XCX starred in “The Moment,” a mockumentary that pits the singer against record-company executives who want it to be “Brat Summer Forever.” The marketing plan seems designed to gall Charli, who has made a career out of hard pivots and clean breaks with past versions of herself. Yet the suits might be on to something. Even on a burning planet, it can’t be summer forever. But it can be in a pop song. The stupid wisdom of “Brat Summer Forever” lies in how it recognizes the tricks that pop music plays with time: with one hand, suspending it and, with the other, marking it out for us in neat segments.

In May, a few months after “The Moment” was released, ahead of a summer without a name—Heat-Dome Summer? Red-Sun Summer? Cyclosporiasis Summer?—Charli made a heel turn that would have confounded the fictional label bosses. “Rock Music,” the first single from her upcoming album “Music, Fashion, Film,” marked the end of Brat Summer and the beginning of something else. “I think the dance floor is dead / So now we’re making rock music,” Charli drawls, digitally elongating the vowel in “rock” into a metallic stutter—a “My Generation” moment for the post-hyperpop age. Some fans welcomed what they immediately dubbed the “Charli rock era,” but others wondered if the whole thing was a joke. Even with its ultraprocessed guitars and occasional bursts of drums, “Rock Music” is not quite rock music. But it’s not not rock music. The song tests how far we’re willing to go along with its account of both Charli’s present and our own. Another single, fittingly titled “Wink Wink,” makes the same challenge from a different angle. “I’m not a bad girl anymore, I promise,” the chorus goes, before immediately undercutting itself with an arch “wink wink wink wink.”

These songs poke at our contradictory desires. On balance, we’d prefer pop stars to exist outside of time, preserved exactly as they were at the height of their powers, or during a particularly memorable season of our own lives. The reunited Backstreet Boys, currently in residency at the Sphere, in Las Vegas, offer a telling graphic in their “Into the Millennium” show: the Boys’ faces frozen into a mountainside—the icy rictus of pop monumentality, playing the hits night after night in Ultima Thule. Artists big and small are used to keeping their material on ice, playing their classic albums front to back whenever they get within spitting distance of a significant anniversary. The first two shows of Jay-Z’s recent three-night run at Yankee Stadium celebrated the respective thirtieth and twenty-fifth anniversaries of “Reasonable Doubt” and “The Blueprint,” a fittingly conservative way for him to return to the limelight amid sexual-assault allegations (which he has denied) and lingering questions about his relationship with Diddy. Fans can receive new material with skepticism, if not outright hostility. In response to the announcement of Olivia Rodrigo’s latest album, one fan wrote on Reddit, “I really hope she didn’t grow as an artist. I want the same exact vibe.”

And yet we do expect pop stars to grow. We want them to keep surprising us, collecting new experiences that we can share vicariously through their music. In 2010, Jay Caspian Kang argued that pop divas need adversity in order to achieve greatness: “To be a true diva,” he wrote, “the singer must make us feel her pain”; she must take us on an “emotional journey.” Some sixteen years later, pop Bildung abounds, thanks largely to online fan communities who can weave the most obscure ephemera into epic tales of redemption. See, for example, the jubilant arc of Dua Lipa—less a purveyor of emotional journeys than of bulletproof club bangers and tasteful book recommendations—whose stilted dancing once inspired the infamous backhanded comment: “I love her lack of energy, go girl give us nothing!” Fans crave these lows, if only to make their idols’ eventual victory on the charts all the more satisfying.

The idea of artists reinventing themselves every few years, in art and in life, is, of course, not new. Madonna, the original type of the modern pop star, has made her transformation over the decades into an artistic medium just as supple as her music. For a while, this kind of durational performance was mostly the province of Madonna’s artier heirs, such as Lady Gaga. Today, though, even the most milquetoast artists are positioned as the protagonists of grand story lines, their careers measured not in albums but in eras. “What are all of BTS’s eras in order?,” one fan on a discussion forum asks, as if cramming for a test. 2023 was said to have marked the end of Ed Sheeran’s “mathematics era,” possibly because he ran out of mathematical symbols to title his records. An era encompasses both the music and its surrounding lore: in BTS’s case, the ongoing cinematic universe of their music videos; in Sheeran’s, the longer arc of the singer’s transition from middle-of-the road folk balladry to middle-of-the-road R. & B. Even Dua Lipa’s clumsy dancing ended up being part of her pilgrim’s progress: it signalled a slough of despond that fans call a “flop era.” Taylor Swift’s innovation, with the Eras Tour, was to take this bit of fan-speak and make it the motive principle behind her live show. Swifties have long taken Taylor’s emotional journey to be their own. A show that replayed that journey over a single night would be almost unbearably profound.

In the course of its hundred and forty-nine performances, the Eras Tour literally inscribed itself into geological time, the vibrations from the stomping fans registering on the Richter scale. Night after night, Swift would perform for more than three hours, running back her career one era at a time, each one its own world with distinctive sets, costumes, and colors. Curiously, the show’s rapid jumps in time and mood were nonlinear; there was no narrative conceit holding everything together. The effect was less like watching a time-lapse than hurtling across a social-media feed. Swift herself described her vision for the tour in these terms: “You’re seeing something new every fifteen to thirty seconds, and so it feels like you’re scrolling in an algorithm.”

When the Eras Tour started, in 2023, Swift had been at war with the shadowy entities that owned her recordings—first, the bosses of her former label Big Machine Records, then the mogul Scooter Braun, who bought Big Machine, in 2019. Partially out of spite and partially out of determination to wrest back some control over her music, Swift set out on the quixotic “Taylor’s Version” project, rerecording her classic albums nearly note for note and releasing them through her new home label, Republic Records. In 2025, flush with funds after the tour’s end, Swift finally bought her original masters back from Shamrock Capital, the private-equity firm that had purchased them from Braun.

From one perspective, the Eras Tour was a triumphant celebration of the star’s ability to reclaim her own work. But from another, it was something eerier: a necro-pop spectacle, proof of the exhumed past’s continued dominance over the present. As Tyler Foggatt wrote in this publication, the Eras Tour was “a show fit for a late-career Las Vegas residency.” Fans, Foggatt noted, caught the morbid vibe—as one wrote, “This is what I imagine a farewell concert to be. Like, the last show you do in your life.” When I caught the Eras Tour over live stream, I couldn’t help thinking of a line in a song, by the underappreciated psychedelic-rock band Cotton Mather: “Some can make a career out of just trying to say goodbye.”

The morbidity implicit in the Eras Tour has become explicit in other marquee post-COVID pop tours. The performances on the Weeknd’s mega-selling After Hours til Dawn Tour issue from a ruined post-apocalyptic cityscape; the singer, flanked by red-cloaked dancers reminiscent of imperial guards from “Star Wars,” dons a mask and acts out a vague story line that plays his career loosely in reverse. Katy Perry’s Lifetimes Tour, performed on an infinity-sign-shaped stage, imagined a campier apocalypse: a cyborg version of Perry fights an evil A.I. that is exterminating the world’s butterflies, summoning her classic outfits and set pieces along the way. Unlike Swift, these artists use narrative devices to give some connective tissue to the succession of hits. These devices seem to share a conviction, however vague or coded, that the present is a wasteland bereft of life and color. The only hope for redemption is to borrow vitality from the past.

Maybe future historians will look back on the pop mega-tours of this moment and see obvious COVID symptoms. The pandemic, after all, sliced history definitively into an unknowing before, an interminable during, and a maybe-one-day after. The return to a golden age of normalcy was one of the most powerful pandemic-era fantasies. But COVID’s fingerprint on the Eras era may also be more direct. Ticket prices for the top world tours spiked some fifty per cent between 2019 and 2024, significantly outpacing inflation. By the time venues reopened, touring artists were returning to a market where live shows had become more of an exclusive luxury product than ever before. Perhaps the only way to give fans their money’s worth was to make the cataclysm they’d lived through feel like an epic shared history.

Then again, too much history all at once can give you amnesia. History, the late literary critic Fredric Jameson did not quite say, is what hits you in the head. Overwhelmed fans reported blacking out at the Eras Tour, all memories of the night dumped. (Swift later joked that she was delighted to hear this: “I think we did it!” she said on Travis Kelce’s podcast.) All the more fitting, then, that amnesia is the central theme in Ariana Grande’s Eternal Sunshine Tour, under way this summer. The narrative frame for the tour, Grande’s first since 2019, is a gloomy sci-fi conceit reminiscent of those of Perry’s and the Weeknd’s shows. In a series of video interludes that break up the performance into acts, Grande plays Peaches, a woman who wants to undergo a procedure to erase her painful memories. (Grande has explored this character before, both in music videos and in the 2025 short film “Brighter Days Ahead,” a companion to her 2024 album and a tribute to Michel Gondry’s “Eternal Sunshine of the Spotless Mind.”) Peaches, we gather, is a singer, and we are encouraged to imagine Grande’s live performance as an enactment of Peaches’s memories.

It’s hard not to see the whole concept as an allegory for the tragedy that has marked Grande’s own life. Between the deadly suicide bombing at her concert in Manchester, in 2017, and the 2018 death of her close friend and ex-boyfriend Mac Miller, just months after the two separated, she no doubt has more than her share of things she’d rather forget. Still, the Eternal Sunshine Tour is bullish on the past. At the climax of the show, having seen the value in her past experiences, Peaches decides that she doesn’t want to go through with the procedure. (It’s essentially a heady reiteration of her breezy 2019 single “Thank U, Next.”) After a few more songs, the show concludes with Grande being beamed up into a giant ring-shaped screen suspended over the stage, where she vanishes; on the screen, Peaches and her older and younger selves have a final reconciliation. It should have been morbid or cheesy, but the visual delight of seeing the singer lifted into the air—all while she riffs acrobatically over “Supernatural”—obliterates any skepticism. The sheer vocal power Grande calls from somewhere in her fragile-looking body lifts the gloom and lets the sunshine in. For a moment, the past seems not to weigh on the present but to float above it like a halo.

Or maybe it keeps playing on a loop. Whereas Grande’s assumption is the most visually astonishing part of the show, the most compelling musical performance of the night comes during “Eternal Sunshine.” Grande begins the song by looping a series of vocal lines, a cappella and live. As the loops build, the lines glance off one another, ricocheting back and forth—an on-the-nose but effective arrangement for a song about being in a holding pattern. “Get me out of this loop,” she sings at one point—and, later, “I try to wipe my mind.” Another allegory briefly peeks through: maybe the cycle she’s trapped in is nothing less than the greatest-hits reel itself, the imperative to keep playing the old songs. Maybe it would be better to give us nothing than to give us the triumphal procession of one era after another.

One era after another is not a bad way to describe the narrative arc of Billy Joel’s “We Didn’t Start the Fire,” a song that arrived in 1989, right at the supposed end of history. The late poet and scholar Joshua Clover wrote about the queasy sublimity of that song’s vision of history, how its speed run of the previous four decades’ events ends up making the present feel inert and paralyzing: “This experience of immutable endlessness, of exploded time and a superfluity of history in the face of which meaningful action is impossible—this is the secret sense of the period in pop music.” Today’s period-obsessed pop feels this stasis, too. Its most arresting images reflect Clover’s sense of immutable endlessness: Swift’s amnesia-inducing feed of memories, Perry’s infinity-shaped stage, Grande’s ascent to the big circular screen in the sky.

And then we have Charli, whose new songs take the endless void in stride. “Spring, Summer ’26 / When the world is gonna end, no hope for any of it,” she sings over spare guitar and drums, in her new indie-rock mode. “Yeah, we’re walking on a runway that goes straight to hell / Nothing’s gonna save us, not music, fashion, or film.” The chord progression loops without resolving, only briefly grazing the tonic in passing: walk, walk, turn, walk, walk, turn. The end is nigh, but endlessly deferred. It’s a slow apocalypse, but it’s also a fashion show. ♦

title: This, Too, Shall Pass
author: Carolyn Wells
content:
Linni Kral has always been preoccupied with her bowels, but as a food writer, it hasn’t usually been that end she’s focused on in her writing. Now, as the internet explodes with “scat chat,” Kral is ready to investigate whether obsessing over our bowel movements has any merit. The result is a giggle fest—though you’ll need the stomach for some serious poo talk.

One day, it seems, the internet woke up and chose BMs, and suddenly the hottest girl you know is posting about scat. Now you have to go out of your way to not eat fiber—prebiotic supplements are in our soda, our candy bars, our cold foam. The beverage case is dominated by the likes of Olipop and Poppi and Culture Pop, all offering varying degrees of digestive assistance. The other day, I saw a smoothie blend in the freezer aisle called “Fiber Supremacy,” and earlier this year, Frito-Lay launched a fiber-packed version of both SunChips and Smartfood popcorn. Kraft is making a purgative macaroni and cheese that boasts six grams of fiber per serving (or 15 grams if you eat the whole box—which is, let’s be honest, how most people consume Easy Mac). Outside the retail space, home cooks are finding ways to fit chia and flax into not just their breakfasts but their meat loaf. They’re pureeing beans into sauces and veggies into puddings and cakes. Literal doctors are posting their #fibermaxxing menus to TikTok. And while this may sound like just another wave on the ocean of content we surf daily, it gets…weirder.

title: The Beauty of a Stone Wall
author: Brendan Fitzgerald
content:
By the time I encountered the fifth photo in Matt Seaton’s contemplative essay about New England’s stone walls, I found myself participating in the image, trying to figure out the maneuvers that had made the structure cohere. That’s a lot of the gratification here—”striving for coherence,” as Seaton, a former Atlantic editor, describes the work of walling. This is a quick read, and Seaton makes every word count, fitting a bit of Robert Frost and a lot of rock knowledge together just like he was building a . . . well, you know.

Bit by bit—which is the way with walls—my interest and knowledge deepened until what had begun as recreation morphed into a hobby job, mending other people’s walls. Eventually, I realized not only that I liked building walls, but also that I could scratch a subsistence living at it. In what probably struck friends and family as an act of lunacy, I quit my day job as an editor at this magazine and became a part-time waller.
